questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define density and state its unit. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine the density of a piece of stone (irregularly-shaped object). Include in your description:

- a list of apparatus needed
- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure you will use to collect data
- how the data is used to obtain the density of the stone
- any precaution taken to minimize error. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Density is the **mass per unit volume** of a substance: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$. Its SI unit is $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ (also $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$).

(ii) **Apparatus:** electronic balance (or beam balance and masses), measuring cylinder, water, thread, the stone, paper towel.

**Diagram:**

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_1.png)

**Procedure:**

1. Measure the mass $m$ of the dry stone on the balance.
2. Half-fill the measuring cylinder with water and read the volume $V_1$, with the eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.
3. Tie the stone to the thread and lower it slowly into the water until it is completely immersed.
4. Read the new volume $V_2$.

**Use of the data:** the volume of the stone is the volume of water displaced, $V = V_2 - V_1$. Then the density is

$\rho = \dfrac{m}{V_2 - V_1}$

**Precautions:** read the meniscus at eye level to avoid parallax error; lower the stone gently to avoid splashing; make sure no air bubbles cling to the stone and that it is fully covered by water; use a cylinder narrow enough to give a readable volume change; repeat the experiment and take the average.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define pressure. *[1 mark]*

A rectangular block $0.01\,\mathrm{m}$ by $0.02\,\mathrm{m}$ by $0.04\,\mathrm{m}$ has a mass of $0.064\,\mathrm{kg}$. Calculate:

(ii) the area of the largest face of the block; *[2 marks]*

(iii) the weight of the block; *[2 marks]*

(iv) the pressure the block will exert on a surface when lying on its largest face. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Pressure is the **force acting normally (perpendicularly) per unit area**: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$. Unit: pascal ($\mathrm{Pa} = \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$).

(ii) Largest face: $0.02 \times 0.04 = 8\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.

(iii) Weight $W = mg = 0.064 \times 10 = 0.64\,\mathrm{N}$.

(iv) $P = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{0.64}{8\times10^{-4}} = 800\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define elastic limit. *[2 marks]*

(ii) A copper wire is stretched by a force which is gradually increased in magnitude until the wire breaks. Sketch a force-extension graph for the wire. On your graph indicate the elastic limit. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The elastic limit is the **maximum force (or extension) up to which a material returns to its original length when the force is removed**. Beyond it the material is permanently deformed.

(ii) **Graph:** force $F$ on the vertical axis, extension $e$ on the horizontal axis. The graph is a **straight line through the origin** (extension proportional to force, Hooke's law) up to the elastic limit. Beyond the elastic limit the graph **curves towards the extension axis**: the wire stretches more and more for each extra newton (copper is ductile) until it **breaks**. Mark the elastic limit at the point where the line stops being straight.

![fig-2](gce-ol-physics-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_2.png)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define a longitudinal wave and give an example. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine the speed of sound in air. Include in your description:

- a list of apparatus needed
- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure you will use to collect data
- how the data is used to obtain the speed of sound
- any precaution taken to minimize error. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A longitudinal wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium **vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels**. Example: **sound**.

(ii) **Echo method.**

**Apparatus:** a long tape measure (or trundle wheel), a stopwatch, a large flat wall (for example a high building), two wooden blocks (or a hand clapper) to make a sharp sound.

**Diagram:**

![fig-3](gce-ol-physics-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_3.png)

**Procedure:**

1. Stand at a measured distance $d$ from the wall (at least about $80\,\mathrm{m}$) and measure $d$ with the tape.
2. Clap the blocks together and start the stopwatch at the clap; stop it when the echo is heard.
3. Repeat several times and take the mean time $t$.

**Use of the data:** the sound travels to the wall and back, a total distance $2d$, in time $t$, so

$v = \dfrac{2d}{t}$

(for example $d = 85\,\mathrm{m}$ and $t = 0.50\,\mathrm{s}$ give $v = 340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$).

**Precautions:** stand far enough from the wall so that the echo is distinct and the time is long enough to measure accurately; repeat and average; make sure the sound is sharp and short; avoid windy days.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define wavelength. *[1 mark]*

Plane waves generated on the surface of a ripple tank are found to travel $0.74\,\mathrm{m}$ in $1.6\,\mathrm{s}$. The distance between a crest and an adjacent trough is $0.06\,\mathrm{m}$. Calculate:

(ii) the average speed of the wave; *[2 marks]*

(iii) the wavelength of the wave; *[2 marks]*

(iv) the frequency of the wave. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Wavelength is the **distance between two successive crests (or two successive troughs)**, that is, the length of one complete wave.

(ii) $v = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{0.74}{1.6} = 0.4625 \approx 0.46\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(iii) A crest and the adjacent trough are **half a wavelength** apart, so $\lambda = 2\times 0.06 = 0.12\,\mathrm{m}$.

(iv) $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.4625}{0.12} = 3.85 \approx 3.9\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define the principal focus of a converging lens. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Draw a ray diagram to show how a converging lens is used as a magnifying glass. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The principal focus is the **point on the principal axis to which rays travelling parallel to the axis (and close to it) converge after refraction through the lens**.

(ii) Place the object **between the lens and its principal focus** $F$. Draw a first ray from the top of the object **parallel to the principal axis**; after the lens it is refracted **through the principal focus** on the far side. Draw a second ray from the top of the object **through the optical centre**, which goes straight on without bending. The two refracted rays **diverge**, so trace them back (dotted lines): they appear to come from a point on the object's side of the lens, farther from the lens than the object. An eye on the far side sees a **virtual, upright, magnified image**.

![fig-4](gce-ol-physics-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_4.png)
